guideTitle: The Best Monitor Arms for Ultrawide and Super-Ultrawide Screens
metaTitle: Best Ultrawide Monitor Arms for 34- to 49-Inch Screens (2026)
metaDescription: Screen size, bare-panel weight and VESA pattern decide which arm can hold an ultrawide. We compared six arms rated from 34 to 57 inches on load, VESA, mounting and warranty.
introParagraphs: An ultrawide is harder to mount than a standard monitor. Three numbers have to line up: the arm's rated screen size, its weight range against your monitor's bare-panel weight without the stand, and the VESA pattern on the back of the screen. A 34-inch ultrawide and a 49-inch super-ultrawide often differ on all three.

Curved panels add another consideration: their weight can sit further forward than a flat panel's, so an arm with some margin above your monitor's weight is the more cautious choice. Several manufacturers here describe reinforced designs for that reason.
The six arms below run from about $30 to about $400 at the time of writing. Our comparison is based on published specifications, load ratings, VESA support and warranties, not hands-on testing.

wali-heavy-duty-single-monitor-arm.summary: An aluminum gas-spring arm rated for 17- to 49-inch screens up to 33 lb, with clamp or grommet mounting.
wali-heavy-duty-single-monitor-arm.description:
The WALI is the least expensive way to mount an ultrawide: it is rated for 17- to 49-inch screens up to 33 lb, at about $30 at the time of writing.

It is aluminum with a gas spring for height adjustment and 360-degree rotation, mounts by C-clamp or grommet, and has a three-year warranty. WALI describes a "Zero-Drift" design intended to stop the monitor sinking after setup.

Its 33 lb limit is the lowest among the 49-inch-rated arms here, so check your monitor's bare-panel weight carefully if it's a heavy curved 49-inch model.
pros: Lowest price here at the time of writing
cons: Lowest load rating of the 49-inch arms
VESA pattern not stated in the listing summary
Less buyer feedback than the Ergotron arms
wali-heavy-duty-single-monitor-arm.bestFor: Lighter 34-inch ultrawides on a tight budget.
wali-heavy-duty-single-monitor-arm.skipIf: Your 49-inch monitor is close to 33 lb without its stand; the ARES WING is rated to 44 lb.

ares-wing-ultrawide-monitor-desk-arm.summary: A gas-spring arm rated for 17 to 49 inches and 44 lb, with listed Odyssey G9 compatibility.
ares-wing-ultrawide-monitor-desk-arm.description:
The ARES WING is the value pick for a 49-inch screen: it is rated for 17 to 49 inches and up to 44 lb, and ARES WING lists compatibility with the Samsung Odyssey G9 and LG super-ultrawides.

It uses an industrial gas spring, mounts by C-clamp or grommet and has a three-year warranty.

It matches the TitanLift's load rating for less, but without the TitanLift's reinforced design or five-year warranty. Confirm your monitor's VESA pattern against the included plate.
specs: Listed compatibility: Samsung Odyssey G9, LG super-ultrawides
pros: 44 lb rating at a mid-range price
cons: VESA range not stated in the listing summary
ares-wing-ultrawide-monitor-desk-arm.bestFor: Mounting a 49-inch super-ultrawide without paying Ergotron prices.
ares-wing-ultrawide-monitor-desk-arm.skipIf: You want the longest warranty in this price range; the TitanLift lists five years.

huanuo-titanlift-heavy-duty-monitor-arm.summary: A reinforced aluminum arm rated for 49 inches and 44 lb, with a five-year warranty.
huanuo-titanlift-heavy-duty-monitor-arm.description:
The TitanLift is designed around heavy curved panels: HUANUO says its arm is 20% thicker and its base 30% wider than its standard model, and that it has been tested through 50,000 movement cycles. It is rated for screens up to 49 inches and 44 lb.

It is aluminum, mounts with a dual C-clamp and carries a five-year warranty.

It costs more than the ARES WING with the same load rating, and the dual clamp needs enough clear desk edge. The listing doesn't mention a grommet option.
cons: Costs more than the ARES WING
Dual clamp needs clear desk edge
huanuo-titanlift-heavy-duty-monitor-arm.bestFor: A heavy curved 34- to 49-inch panel where margin and warranty matter.
huanuo-titanlift-heavy-duty-monitor-arm.skipIf: You need a grommet mount; the ARES WING offers one at the same rating.

ergotron-lx-monitor-arm.summary: Ergotron's LX, rated for 34-inch flat or curved screens from 7 to 25 lb, with a 10-year warranty.
ergotron-lx-monitor-arm.description:
The Ergotron LX is the pick for a 34-inch ultrawide, and only up to that size: it is rated for 34-inch flat or curved panels weighing 7 to 25 lb, with VESA 75 x 75 or 100 x 100mm.

It offers 13 inches of lift, 360-degree rotation and 75 degrees of tilt, and carries a 10-year warranty, tied with the HX for the longest here.

It is not rated for 49-inch super-ultrawides, and its VESA range won't fit monitors that need 200 x 200mm.
pros: Established brand with extensive buyer feedback
cons: Costs more than the 49-inch-rated budget arms
ergotron-lx-monitor-arm.bestFor: 34-inch ultrawides under 25 lb, where a long warranty matters.
ergotron-lx-monitor-arm.skipIf: You have a 49-inch screen; the Ergotron HX or ARES WING is rated for it.

ergotron-hx-premium-heavy-duty-monitor-a.summary: Ergotron's heavy-duty arm for flat or slightly curved screens up to 49 inches and 20 to 42 lb.
ergotron-hx-premium-heavy-duty-monitor-a.description:
The Ergotron HX is the choice for a heavy 49-inch screen that needs 200 x 200mm VESA: it supports that pattern and is rated for flat or slightly curved panels up to 49 inches, weighing 20 to 42 lb.

It offers 11.5 inches of lift and 360-degree rotation, with a 10-year warranty.

Note the rating's wording: flat or slightly curved. If your panel has a tight curve, check Ergotron's compatibility guidance. It is also the most expensive Ergotron here, and its 20 lb minimum rules out lighter monitors.
specs: Screen size: up to 49" (flat or slightly curved)
cons: Rated for flat or slightly curved panels
Costs far more than the ARES WING
ergotron-hx-premium-heavy-duty-monitor-a.bestFor: Heavy 49-inch monitors with a 200 x 200mm VESA pattern.
ergotron-hx-premium-heavy-duty-monitor-a.skipIf: Your monitor is under 20 lb; the Ergotron LX suits a lighter 34-inch panel.

secretlab-magnus-monitor-arm-heavy-duty.badge: Best for Screens Up to 57 Inches
secretlab-magnus-monitor-arm-heavy-duty.summary: Secretlab's heavy-duty arm rated up to 57 inches and 18 to 35 lb, with magnetic cable management.
secretlab-magnus-monitor-arm-heavy-duty.description:
The Secretlab Magnus Heavy Duty is the only arm here rated beyond 49 inches: Secretlab rates it for ultrawide gaming monitors up to 57 inches, weighing 18 to 35 lb.

It uses a tensile spring Secretlab says is designed for curved gaming panels, and its magnetic cable management keeps cables in the arm.

Its weight limit is lower than the ARES WING, TitanLift or HX, so a very heavy panel may still exceed it despite the size rating. It was also the most expensive arm here at the time of writing, with less buyer feedback than the Ergotron arms.
pros: Designed for curved gaming panels (per Secretlab)
cons: Most expensive here at the time of writing
35 lb limit is lower than several cheaper arms
Less buyer feedback than the Ergotron arms
secretlab-magnus-monitor-arm-heavy-duty.bestFor: 57-inch gaming monitors, or a gaming desk where cable management matters.
secretlab-magnus-monitor-arm-heavy-duty.skipIf: Your panel weighs more than 35 lb; the ARES WING, TitanLift or HX has a higher limit.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Compare the monitor's weight without its stand, from its spec sheet, against the arm's range. Ranges here run from 7 to 25 lb (Ergotron LX) up to 44 lb (ARES WING, TitanLift).
Many 34-inch ultrawides use 100 x 100mm; some larger screens need 200 x 200mm, which the Ergotron HX supports. Check your monitor and the arm's plate.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Check both size and weight ratings
buyingCriteria.explanation: A size rating doesn't guarantee capacity. The Secretlab is rated for 57-inch screens but only up to 35 lb.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Confirm your desk can take the mount
buyingCriteria.explanation: Clamps need a solid edge of suitable thickness, and grommet mounts need a hole. Hollow-core or glass desktops may not suit either; check the arm's desk requirements.

faq.q: Can a standard monitor arm hold a 49-inch ultrawide?
faq.a: Only if it is rated for the screen's size and bare-panel weight and fits its VESA pattern. Many standard arms are not; the arms here rated for 49 inches include the WALI, ARES WING, TitanLift and Ergotron HX.

faq.q: Does a curved ultrawide need a sturdier arm?
faq.a: A curved panel's weight can sit further forward than a flat one's, which adds leverage on the arm. Choosing an arm with some margin above your monitor's weight is the cautious approach.
Check your monitor's specifications. Many 34-inch ultrawides use 100 x 100mm; some larger monitors use 200 x 200mm.
The Ergotron LX is rated for 34-inch panels from 7 to 25 lb, with a 10-year warranty. The WALI is the lower-cost alternative.
A clamp needs a solid desk edge and is easy to move; a grommet mount needs a hole but keeps the edge clear. The WALI and ARES WING list both.

bottomLine: For a 34-inch ultrawide, the Ergotron LX is the long-warranty choice, with the WALI as a low-cost alternative. For a 49-inch super-ultrawide, the ARES WING offers a 44 lb rating for the money, and the TitanLift adds a reinforced design and five-year warranty.
The Ergotron HX is for heavy 49-inch panels that need 200 x 200mm VESA, and the Secretlab Magnus is the only arm here rated to 57 inches, as long as your monitor is within its 35 lb limit.
